description: HumanOrbit is a team passionate about space exploration, science, and technology. We believe innovation begins with understanding real challenges and finding creative ways to solve them. Through our project ECHO, we combine research, software development, and artificial intelligence to explore new ways of protecting astronaut health, improving crew safety, and supporting future human missions beyond Earth.
summary:
A spacecraft can have an environmental problem before every astronaut shows signs of distress. Carbon dioxide may begin rising in one area while a crew member's oxygen saturation still looks normal. Minutes later, a second area may show the same trend, but the astronaut there may respond differently. Looking at either person's vital signs alone would miss part of the story.

We developed ECHO (Environmental & Crew Health Observer), a web-based prototype designed to connect astronaut health data with environmental readings from different spacecraft zones. ECHO compares what is changing in the cabin with what is changing in each crew member, considering their location, activity, and recent trends. A rule-based assessment engine identifies patterns that deserve attention, while the ECHO conversational assistant explains the evidence, its limitations, and the appropriate next checks in plain language.

Our demonstration uses public physiological datasets and simulated environmental scenarios. ECHO is not a replacement for NASA's medical or life-support systems. It explores how information already collected by spaceflight technologies could become more useful when interpreted together, for the whole crew.
details:
Our Solution and How It Works

We created ECHO (Environmental & Crew Health Observer) because we wanted astronauts to have a clearer picture of their health and what is happening around them during a mission.

ECHO is a working web platform that receives a continuous stream of physiological and environmental telemetry through WebSockets, allowing measurements and graphs to update in real time. The dashboard displays heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, skin temperature, blood pressure, and other cardiovascular indicators, alongside cabin CO₂, temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure. But our idea was not just to put these values on a screen. We wanted to connect them with the conditions inside the spacecraft and see how different astronauts might respond to the same situation.

With this in mind, we included a Crew Overview section, where we can monitor the latest health status of all three astronauts in one place. It shows their vital signs, current condition, and active alerts, while keeping each astronaut's monitoring history separate. This allows us to quickly see who may need attention without having to review each profile individually.

To make this possible, we developed a deterministic evaluation engine. It receives the measurements, checks their validity, and evaluates them using predefined thresholds. When the data meets certain conditions, the system generates an alert and identifies what caused it. We decided to use this approach so that the evaluation follows established rules instead of leaving medical interpretations entirely to artificial intelligence.

To make this process more transparent, we added a Rule Inspector. It allows us to see which rules are being evaluated, the thresholds they use, their results, and the conditions required for an alert to clear. This way, we can understand not only when ECHO generates an alert, but also the exact reason behind it.

We also included an AI-powered assistant that makes the information easier to understand. Astronauts can ask about their measurements, understand why an alert was generated, and receive recommendations and guidance based on the available information and authorized procedures.

Demonstration and Emergency Response

We wanted to test ECHO in situations that astronauts might encounter, including moments when the measurements change unexpectedly or the system stops receiving information.

For this reason, we developed five scenarios that we can control during the demonstration:

  1. Resting Baseline: We observe how ECHO monitors an astronaut when physiological measurements remain stable.
  2. High Exertion: Heart rate, respiratory rate, and movement increase, allowing us to see how the system handles changes associated with physical activity.
  3. Oxygenation Disturbance: SpO₂ decreases progressively, showing how ECHO recognizes the change and generates alerts at different levels.
  4. Combined Physiological Event: Heart rate, estimated systolic blood pressure, and movement change simultaneously. This helps us evaluate how the system responds when several indicators are affected together.
  5. Telemetry Failure: We interrupt the flow of measurements to check whether ECHO identifies missing or outdated data and recovers when valid readings return.

These scenarios helped us go beyond simply displaying information. We can observe how the evaluation engine behaves, what causes an alert to appear, and whether the monitoring history remains available when something goes wrong.

We also thought about what would happen if astronauts needed assistance while communication with Earth was unavailable. Our proposal includes preparing reports of important events so that medical teams and Mission Control could review them once communication is restored.

Proposed Hardware Ecosystem

While working on ECHO, we explored how our platform could eventually connect with technologies already developed for astronaut health monitoring.

One of them is the Canadian Space Agency's Bio-Monitor, which uses AstroSkin wearable technology to record cardiovascular and respiratory measurements.

We propose complementing this system with an environmental sensor module capable of measuring CO₂ partial pressure, oxygen concentration, and atmospheric pressure. Our intention is to connect information about the astronaut's body with the conditions in the surrounding environment.

We also designed the concept of a wristband that would make it easier for astronauts to interact with the platform during their daily routines.

Instead of opening the dashboard every time they need to update their information, astronauts could use this wristband to register their current activity.

They could also indicate their location inside the International Space Station, including modules such as Destiny, Columbus, and Kibo. Knowing the astronaut's activity and location would give ECHO more context when interpreting physiological changes and environmental conditions.

The wristband would also receive notifications and alerts, helping astronauts stay informed without constantly checking the main platform.

Technologies, Programming Languages, and Tools

To develop ECHO, we used a combination of technologies for the dashboard, data processing, communication between components, and testing.

Backend and Data Processing

  • Python
  • FastAPI and Pydantic
  • SQLModel and SQLite
  • HTTP APIs and WebSockets
  • Persistent telemetry storage, data validation, and deterministic alert rules

Frontend and Visualization

  • React and TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Recharts for graphs and monitoring history
  • Lucide for interface icons

Simulation and Testing

  • An independent telemetry simulator built with Python
  • Five configurable scenarios
  • Deterministic monitoring profiles and adjustable thresholds
  • Playwright for end-to-end testing
  • Automated scripts for configuration and system validation

Development and Infrastructure

  • Docker and Docker Compose
  • Git and GitHub
  • OpenAPI documentation
  • Environment configuration and persistent Docker volumes

Scientific Data

We researched scientific datasets and NASA environmental records to understand the physiological and environmental measurements relevant to ECHO. We also obtained historical environmental telemetry from NASA's RR-1 mission as part of our research.

For our current demonstration, we developed a Python simulator that continuously generates synthetic telemetry. This allows us to reproduce different physiological conditions, test the evaluation engine, and observe how the dashboard, alerts, and monitoring history respond as new data arrives. The downloaded NASA records have not yet been integrated into the backend.

Innovation and Intended Impact

The idea behind ECHO came from something we consider important: knowing an astronaut's vital signs is useful, but those numbers become more meaningful when we understand the situation in which they were recorded.

For instance, a higher heart rate during exercise does not necessarily mean the same thing as a higher heart rate while resting. In the same way, if several crew members experience physiological changes around the same time, it may be worth looking at the environmental conditions they share.

We wanted our platform to consider those differences. That is why ECHO connects physiological measurements with environmental information and evaluates both individual astronauts and the crew as a whole. The deterministic engine identifies conditions that require attention, while the AI assistant helps explain the results in a way astronauts can understand.

Another important consideration was the distance from Earth. During long missions, astronauts may face situations where they cannot immediately consult a medical team. Being able to review their measurements, understand an alert, and access guidance based on authorized procedures could help them respond more confidently.

Our goal is for ECHO to help astronauts understand their health, recognize changes that deserve attention, and look after one another as a crew, even when support from Earth is not immediately available.
